title: Optimal randomized competitive ratio of weighted k-server
formal: Determine the asymptotic growth of \(R_{w}(k)\), the optimal randomized competitive ratio of the weighted k-server problem over all finite uniform metrics, up to universal multiplicative constants as the integer k tends to infinity. Use an oblivious request adversary and expected online cost, as defined below.

source_formulation.text: Closing the exponential gap between the 1.62 upper bound and the \(\Omega (2k )\) lower bound on the randomized competitive ratio is still an open problem.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 3

context:
Even with all locations equally far apart, deciding when to move an expensive rather than a cheap server creates a substantial online uncertainty cost.

The SODA 2026 result gives an \(\exp (O(k^{2}))\)-competitive randomized algorithm. Thus merely asking whether randomization can beat a doubly-exponential bound would now retain an answered target.

The exponential lower bound and the \(\exp (O(k^{2}))\) upper bound leave the optimal randomized ratio undetermined. The retained card asks for that full function, independently of the decomposition method motivating the older occurrence.

The 2023 source contains an earlier randomized weighted-k-server question. The 2026 upper bound supersedes the qualitative doubly-exponential barrier; its bibliography is retained here under the current optimal-ratio target.

sentences: Weighted k-server assigns a separate movement-cost multiplier to each server.
All distinct locations are at unit distance, isolating uncertainty about which weight to move.
The target is the optimal randomized competitive ratio as a function of the number of servers.
It takes the worst case over finite metric sizes and arbitrary positive weights against oblivious requests.
The recent \(\exp (O(k^{2}))\) upper bound removes the old doubly-exponential barrier but leaves a substantial gap above exponential lower bounds.

definitions: For \(k\ge 1\) an instance environment consists of a finite set X with |\(X|\ge k+1\), uniform distance \(d(x,y)=1\) if \(x\ne y\) and 0 otherwise, positive real weights \(w_{1},\ldots ,w_{k}\), and an initial location \(c_{i}\in X\) for each labeled server i. Co-location is permitted. These data are known to the online algorithm. A finite request sequence \(\sigma \in X\)* is revealed one request at a time. Before proceeding, at least one server must occupy the requested location. Moving server i from x to y costs \(w_{i} d(x,y)\); all movements count. The algorithm may use arbitrary computation but cannot inspect future requests. \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )\) is the minimum cost of an offline execution with the same weights and initial locations. A real \(c\ge 1\) is universally achievable for k if, for every environment, there are a randomized online strategy A and \(b\ge 0\) such that for every finite \(\sigma , E[\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma )]\le c \operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )+b\). The strategy and b may depend on the environment; b may not depend on \(\sigma\) or its length. The sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s private random choices, and expectation is over those choices. Define \(R_{w}(k)\) as the infimum of universally achievable c. It is finite by known upper bounds and need not be attained. Metric size and the ratios between server weights are unbounded independently of k. No running-time bound or bit encoding of the real weights is imposed; the target measures online movement cost.
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(k)\) and constants \(a,A>0,k_{0}\) such that a \(g(k)\le R_{w}(k)\le A g(k)\) for every integer \(k\ge k_{0}\), proving both bounds in the specified randomized model. Constants must not depend on metric size or weights. An improvement for one algorithm, fixed weight ratios or a bounded number of locations does not by itself determine this worst-case function. Precision is multiplicative constant factors in \(R_{w}\), not additive 0.01 and not merely constant factors in its logarithm.
